title: Interpolative Separable Density-Fitting for Transcorrelated Hamiltonians
authors: Ke Liao, Yifan Cheng, Werner Dobrautz, Tianyu Zhu, Ali Alavi
abstract: The transcorrelated (TC) method dramatically accelerates the convergence of correlated calculations toward the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit by folding a Jastrow correlator into the Hamiltonian via a similarity transformation, incorporating the electron--electron cusp into the effective interaction. We make the TC framework practical for large systems and flexible, multi-center correlators by compressing the grid-evaluated TC integrals with the interpolative separable density-fitting (ISDF) approximation, combined with the effective two-body (xTC) treatment of the three-body operator. This low-rank representation reduces storage and integration costs by orders of magnitude, and a multi-GPU implementation with automatic differentiation of the correlator makes the construction routine for large basis sets. We demonstrate the resulting ISDF-xTC-CCSD method on the linear hydrogen chain, reaching the joint thermodynamic and CBS limits with basis sets up to cc-pV5Z in agreement with state-of-the-art many-body references to within about 1~mHa/atom, and on the benzene ground-state energy with up to 1200 orbitals (cc-pCV5Z), where the method attains state-of-the-art accuracy at the coupled cluster singles and doubles level and its CBS extrapolation is markedly more robust than that of conventional coupled-cluster methods.
summary: This paper introduces ISDF-xTC-CCSD, a novel computational framework designed to accurately calculate electron correlation energies by combining the Transcorrelated method with Interpolative Separable Density-Fitting. By compressing complex integrals into low-rank forms, it drastically reduces computational cost while maintaining high accuracy, allowing reliable extrapolation to the Complete Basis Set limit for large molecular systems.
main_problem: The primary challenge is accurately calculating electron correlation energies, especially ensuring convergence towards the Complete Basis Set (CBS) limit for large molecular systems.
main_result: The proposed ISDF-xTC-CCSD method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on benzene and the linear hydrogen chain, demonstrating a significantly more robust CBS extrapolation than conventional coupled-cluster methods.
method: It combines the Transcorrelated (TC) Hamiltonian approach with an effective two-body ($	ext{xTC}$) treatment of three-body operators, utilizing Interpolative Separable Density-Fitting (ISDF) to reduce computational scaling for grid integrals.
model_or_system: The method is applied to electronic structure calculations for molecules like benzene and the linear hydrogen chain. The underlying physics involves treating electron correlation via a Jastrow factor incorporated into the Hamiltonian ($ ar{H}$).
key_observables: Basis-set convergence towards the CBS limit; ground-state energy ($E_{	ext{corr,CBS}}$) for specific molecules.
important_parameters: High basis set levels (up to cc-pV5Z); large system sizes (up to 1200 orbitals in benzene).
main_assumptions: The ISDF approximation assumes that grid-evaluated integrals possess a low-rank structure, allowing for efficient tensor compression and calculation.
figures_summary: Figures compare the per-atom energy deviation from high-level references (like AFQMC+DMRG) across different bond separations for the hydrogen chain, and show the CBS extrapolation of benzene energy relative to the Hartree-Fock limit.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for efficient correlation treatment using TC methods. It then details how ISDF is applied to compress the necessary grid integrals (K and xTC terms). Finally, it presents benchmark calculations on model systems to validate accuracy and convergence properties.
why_interesting: While focused on molecular quantum chemistry, the core techniques—low-rank approximation of complex correlation operators and achieving high-accuracy CBS extrapolation—are highly relevant for developing scalable methods in strongly correlated solid-state materials simulations.
